policy_title: Reform Disability Benefits and Capability for Work Assessments
stated: The Conservative Party will reform disability benefits for better targeting and mental health provision, improve PIP assessments, and tighten how the benefits system assesses capability for work from September 2025 to provide tailored support for those with moderate conditions to engage with work.

source.quote: Reform our disability benefits so they are better targeted and reflect people’s genuine needs... Tighten up how the benefits system assesses capability for work. ...We will change the assessments from September 2025 so that those with more moderate mental health issues or mobility problems who could potentially engage with the world of work are given tailored support...

bearing_set.reason: Tightening PIP eligibility and work-capability criteria would directly reduce income for disabled households currently receiving benefits, materially affecting disposable income and ability to afford essentials.

Reforming work-capability assessments to steer people with moderate conditions toward employment directly determines job-readiness expectations, conditionality, and the nature of support offered — a real verdict on earnings security and employment quality for this group.

'Better targeting' and tighter assessments are explicitly a cost-control measure; reducing the disability benefits caseload reduces current-year expenditure and shifts the funded/borrowed balance — a material effect on fiscal sustainability indicators.

Disability benefit recipients are concentrated in lower-income deciles; cutting or tightening benefits for this group while others are unaffected widens the income gap between bottom and rest — a mechanistic inequality effect.

membership_note: Four fundamentals cleared the non-negligible bar: O2 (loss of benefits directly hits affordability of essentials), O4 (work-engagement component explicitly targets labour market participation/quality for disabled claimants), O12 (explicit spending-reduction intent improves fiscal position), and O14 (cuts fall disproportionately on lower-income disabled households, widening the gap). O3 was considered but 'mental health provision' here refers to benefit-assessment design, not NHS capacity. O13 was considered but the aggregate labour-supply effect routes through O4 at this policy level.
